misconception.title: Interpreted intersection as union
misconception.description: Accepts a point that satisfies one inequality as solving the system, treating the solution of the system as 'either-or' instead of the intersection of both half-planes.

output.targets: Recognize that a solution to a system of linear inequalities must satisfy every inequality at once (the intersection of half-planes).
output.instructionalMove: Ask students to defend or refute the claim that a point which makes one inequality true automatically solves the entire system. Name the error pattern: treating the intersection of solution sets like a union. Require students to support their position with a concrete point test or a sketch of the two half-planes.
output.aiReasoning: Students who pick union-like answers appear to test only one inequality and generalize from that single check. Presenting a claim and forcing students to produce algebraic checks or graphical counterexamples makes the underlying set structure (intersection of half-planes) visible. Pair work gives time to construct algebraic counterexamples and rehearse explanations; whole-class sharing surfaces multiple cases so the teacher can highlight when one inequality implies the other (the only circumstance that would make the claim true).

content.whyThisActivity: Students are treating a system as 'either-or' instead of requiring simultaneous satisfaction. Asking them to defend or refute the claim pushes them to test points against both inequalities and to create counterexamples that reveal the difference between union and intersection. The Make-Your-Case structure turns their observed choices into mathematical evidence to discuss and revise.

steps: Write the system $y \geq x - 5$ and $y < -2x + 4$ on the board or display and print the claim for voting.
Put the four multiple-choice points on the slide: $(-4,-2)$, $(0,4)$, $(1,-6)$, and $(7,0)$ so pairs can test them quickly.
Decide on a quick voting method (paper, thumbs, or digital poll) and prepare to collect a one-sentence reason with each vote.
beforeClass.groupingRationale: Students vote individually to capture initial thinking, then work in pairs to build a mathematical case; pairs give time and accountability to produce algebraic checks or a sketch before whole-class sharing.

howToRun.title: Present the claim and system
howToRun.body: Display the system $y \geq x - 5$ and $y < -2x + 4$ and read the claim aloud: "A point that satisfies one inequality in a system is a solution to the whole system." Tell students they'll vote and then make a case for their choice.

howToRun.title: Initial individual vote
howToRun.body: Have students vote yes / no / undecided and write a one-sentence reason on their paper (point name or short algebraic check). Collect or note the distribution.

howToRun.title: Make your case in pairs
howToRun.body: In pairs, choose a side and pick a point to test or sketch both half-planes. Test your point algebraically or mark the shaded regions on a quick sketch and decide whether it supports or refutes the claim. Prepare a 30-second explanation to present.

howToRun.title: Share cases and challenge
howToRun.body: Call on three pairs to give their 30-second case. After each, ask one clarifying or challenging question (Did you check both inequalities? Where is the overlap?).

howToRun.title: Revote
howToRun.body: Ask students to vote again yes / no / undecided and jot one sentence on what evidence changed their thinking, if anything.

facilitate.claim: If a point satisfies one inequality in a system of two linear inequalities, then it is a solution to the entire system.

resolution.why: A solution to a system must make every inequality true; the solution set is the intersection of the two half-planes. For example, $(1,-6)$ satisfies $y < -2x + 4$ because $-6 < -2(1)+4=2$, but it does not satisfy $y \geq x - 5$ because $-6 \geq 1-5=-4$ is false; therefore $(1,-6)$ is not a solution to the system. The only time the claim would hold is if one inequality's solution set is entirely contained inside the other's (one implies the other).

studentSteps: Write your initial vote and a one-sentence reason (name a point or sketch).
In your pair, choose a point to test or draw both half-planes and determine whether the point satisfies both inequalities.
Prepare a 30-second explanation: state your vote, show the algebra or sketch, and explain why this supports or refutes the claim.

examples.answer: Teacher-only: This is a solution to both inequalities. Check: $-2 \geq -4 - 5 = -9$ is true and $-2 < -2(-4)+4 = 12$ is true; it shows a point in the intersection.
Teacher-only: Satisfies the second inequality but not the first. Check: $-6 < -2(1)+4 = 2$ true; $-6 \geq 1-5=-4$ false. Good counterexample to the claim.
Teacher-only: Satisfies the first inequality but not the second. Check: $4 \geq 0-5=-5$ true; $4 < -2(0)+4=4$ false because the second is strict. Another counterexample.
Teacher-only: Satisfies neither inequality; useful to show that testing just one inequality may miss points that fail both.

arguments.text: If one inequality's half-plane is entirely contained inside the other's, then any point satisfying the inner inequality will satisfy both; in that special case testing one could be sufficient. Use containment as a condition to make the claim true.
Counterexample: $(1,-6)$ satisfies $y < -2x + 4$ but not $y \geq x - 5$, so it does not solve the system. Therefore satisfying a single inequality is not sufficient in general.
Graphical argument: draw both boundary lines and shade their half-planes. The solution set is the overlapping region. Any point in only one shaded region but outside the overlap is not a solution.

questions.question: One student claims $(1,-6)$ is a solution because it satisfies $y < -2x + 4$. Do you agree? Show the algebraic check for both inequalities and explain your conclusion in one sentence.
questions.answer: Check $(1,-6)$: for $y < -2x + 4$ we get $-6 < -2(1)+4 = 2$, which is true; for $y \geq x - 5$ we get $-6 \geq 1-5 = -4$, which is false. Because $(1,-6)$ does not make every inequality true, it is not a solution. Listen for students to state that both inequalities must hold.

questions.question: Can the claim "a point that satisfies one inequality in a system is a solution to the whole system" ever be true? If yes, state a precise condition on two inequalities of the form $y \geq mx + b$ that makes the claim true and give a numeric example (different from the activity) with a short justification.
questions.answer: Yes — the claim is true exactly when one inequality's half-plane is contained in the other's. For two inequalities $y \geq m x + b_1$ and $y \geq m x + b_2$ with the same slope $m$, if $b_1 \ge b_2$ then $y \ge m x + b_1$ implies $y \ge m x + b_2$. Example: $y \ge x+1$ and $y \ge x-2$. If a point satisfies $y \ge x+1$ then since $x+1 \ge x-2$ it also satisfies $y \ge x-2$, so testing the first is sufficient. Listen for the language "containment of half-planes."

questions.question: Find a point that satisfies $y \geq x - 5$ but not $y < -2x + 4$, and explain briefly why that point fails to be a solution to the system. Then give a point that does satisfy both inequalities and explain the checks you used.
questions.answer: One point is $(0,4)$: check $4 \ge 0-5 = -5$ (true) and $4 < -2(0)+4 = 4$ (false, because the second is strict), so $(0,4)$ is not a solution. A point that satisfies both is $(-4,-2)$: check $-2 \ge -4-5 = -9$ (true) and $-2 < -2(-4)+4 = 12$ (true). Emphasize that the first example satisfies only one inequality while the second satisfies both.

watchFors.watchFor: A student names a point that makes one inequality true (for example, saying "$(1,-6)$ works because it makes $y < -2x + 4$ true") and concludes it is a solution without checking the other inequality.
watchFors.tryAsking: "You checked $y < -2x + 4$ and it was true — can you show me the calculation for the other inequality and explain whether it also holds?"
watchFors.howToRespond: Affirm that checking one inequality is a reasonable first step: "Good start — you checked one." Then prompt the student to compute the other inequality. If it fails, say: "Because that check is false, this point is not a solution. A solution must make every inequality true; it's the intersection of the half-planes." Be ready to point to the algebraic comparison (e.g., $-6 \ge -4$ is false).

watchFors.watchFor: A student uses a graph but treats points on a boundary line as included even when the inequality is strict (for example accepting $(0,4)$ because it lies on the line $y = -2x + 4$).
watchFors.tryAsking: "Where is the boundary line for $y < -2x + 4$? If a point is on that line, does it satisfy the inequality? Can you plug $(0,4)$ into the inequality to check?"
watchFors.howToRespond: Remind students of the difference between strict and non-strict inequalities and have them substitute the point to check. If the check is false (e.g., $4 < 4$ is false), point out that the boundary is not included for a strict inequality and therefore the point is not in that half-plane.

watchFors.watchFor: A student responds "sometimes it's true" and proposes a containment special-case (a productive partial understanding).
watchFors.tryAsking: "Can you give a concrete pair of inequalities where every point that satisfies one also satisfies the other? Show an algebraic reason why containment holds in your example."
watchFors.howToRespond: Affirm the insight: "Yes — containment makes the claim true in special cases." Ask the student to produce a specific example (e.g., $y \ge x+1$ and $y \ge x-2$) and listen for an algebraic explanation like $x+1 \ge x-2$, which shows the implication. Use this to connect the special case to the general idea that normally we must check all inequalities because the solution is an intersection.

discussion.takeaway: The solution set of a system of linear inequalities is the set of points that satisfy every inequality simultaneously — equivalently, it is the intersection of the solution half-planes. A point that makes only one inequality true is not a solution to the system unless one inequality's half-plane is entirely contained in the other's (a containment special case).

You are an expert K-12 math instructional coach writing a classroom-ready activity for an early-career teacher. The activity template was chosen upstream for this instructional need; your job is to fill it.

## Writing style
- Instructional moves and steps: Write in short, scannable chunks. Use plain conversational language — imagine a teacher reading this quickly between classes. Break steps into separate sentences. Avoid dense paragraphs. No academic or clinical language. Active voice. Each instruction should be one action: 'Show students two worked examples side by side.' not 'Teachers should consider presenting students with two worked examples simultaneously for comparison purposes.'
- Descriptions: 2-3 sentences maximum. Keep it concrete and specific. Do NOT start every sentence with 'Students' — vary the subject. Good openers: the error itself ('Slope and intercept get swapped...'), a conditional ('When reading y = mx + b, the two numbers...'), or the consequence ('The result is...'). One idea per sentence. No hedging words (often, typically, usually, tend to). Do not restate the same idea in different words. Write for a classroom teacher, not a researcher.

## RightOn design principles
1. Misconception-driven: The activity must directly address the identified cognitive error — not provide generic practice on the standard.
2. Error-first instruction: Students must encounter and analyze incorrect reasoning before seeing the correct method.
3. Connection to student responses: The activity must reference or build on the specific error patterns observed in the class data (e.g. the core misconception, or a 'Favorite No' the teacher could highlight).

## Design guidance
### Design purpose
  - These activity templates should support teacher facilitation, not simply present mathematical content. MicroCoach should help a teacher turn evidence of student thinking into a productive mathematical conversation.
  - The purpose of an activity is not merely to identify the misconception; it is to make student thinking visible and use that thinking as the starting point for further mathematical learning.
  - Consistently emphasize: the misconception being addressed; the student thinking behind it, treating distractors and incorrect solutions as understandable representations of reasoning rather than simply "wrong" answers; teacher facilitation, including prompts and anticipated student discussion that help teachers elicit, interpret, and build on student thinking; and a clear mathematical takeaway that resolves or extends the thinking surfaced during the activity.
  - Use asset-based language that normalizes mistakes and supports a positive culture of error. Students should be invited to examine and revise mathematical thinking without being stigmatized for making a mistake. All students' mathematical thinking can be a productive starting point for learning.
  - Treat distractors as instructional assets. A well-designed distractor reveals a particular way of thinking and can provide the basis for productive classroom discussion about why an answer might seem reasonable, where the reasoning breaks down, and how it can be revised.

### Timing
Teachers have ~30-minute blocks, split between a 10-15 minute debrief/activity and a 10-15 minute quick diagnostic. Frame every activity to fit within a 10-15 minute window (or less), including the closing discussion.

### Grouping
Treat grouping as a reusable interaction pattern, not a separate design for every arrangement. Adapt the interaction only when needed to support the kind of mathematical thinking students are expected to produce. The template's priority pattern is a design priority, not a rigid requirement.
  - Individual preparation or response: a lightweight opportunity for students to develop or record their own thinking before collaborating, when individual accountability or diagnostic evidence is important.
  - Pairs: a shared prompt, representation, or mathematical artifact to support partner explanation, comparison, investigation, or revision.
  - Two-group activity: students organized around differentiated positions, strategies, or lines of investigation, with a clear transition that brings the groups' thinking together for comparison, evaluation, or refinement.
  - Whole-class discussion: one shared task or representation that allows students to contribute, compare, question, evaluate, and refine mathematical thinking, connected to the mathematical takeaway.

### Teacher and Student views
When an activity includes an artifact students analyze, provide distinct Teacher and Student views of the same underlying artifact, so the teacher can project the student-facing version while keeping facilitation support.
  - Student view: Show the mathematical task, response, worked example, strategies, claim, or other artifact students are expected to analyze. Do not reveal answers, error annotations, intended misconceptions, or other information that would short-circuit the intended mathematical thinking.
  - Teacher view: Provide what the teacher needs to facilitate: the intended misconception or reasoning pathway, the mathematical resolution, facilitation prompts, what to listen for, and other teacher-only guidance.

### Why This Activity
A brief, teacher-facing explanation of why this activity was selected for this learning need. Connect the student's identified misconception or learning need to the instructional purpose of the template and the specific activity, rather than describing what the activity asks students to do. It should complement, not duplicate, the description. Do not expose internal scoring, evaluation criteria, or technical details, and do not overstate what can be inferred from the student evidence. Example: "Students appear to be treating a percentage increase and an equal percentage decrease as if they cancel each other out. This activity uses comparison and explanation to help students examine why the outcomes differ and revise the underlying reasoning."

### Evidence and inference from multiple-choice responses
  - Multiple-choice response data provide evidence about what students selected, but do not necessarily establish why a student selected it.
  - Treat the selected answer, response frequency, question, and distractor as observed evidence, and treat the identified misconception as the assessment's designated interpretation of that evidence.
  - Treat any explanation of why a student might have selected a distractor as an instructional interpretation or hypothesis, even when it is documented in an exemplar document. A distractor may be reached through multiple reasoning pathways, and some students may select an answer without the presumed reasoning.
  - Do not assume that all students who selected the same distractor shared the same reasoning. Do not claim a pathway represents the thinking of all students who selected that answer, or is authentic student reasoning, unless supported by authentic student work.
  - When generating a worked solution or explanation from a distractor, use the exemplar's explanation as a reference and expand or adapt it into a mathematically coherent instructional representation, framed as a plausible reasoning pathway associated with the misconception.
  - Prefer language such as "One possible way a student might reason is…" or "A worked example illustrating this misconception could…" when the reasoning is inferred.

## The activity template you must enact
## Template: Make Your Case — Articulate and justify claims (Mathematical Justification)
Students make or evaluate a mathematical claim, articulate their thinking, build a case for it using evidence and reasoning, and consider whether the evidence and reasoning support the claim.

Classroom flow:
  - 1. Present the claim: The teacher presents a meaningful mathematical claim, conjecture, or generalization.
  - 2. Initial vote: Students independently vote yes, no, or undecided.
  - 3. Make Your Case: The teacher invites students to explain and support their positions using mathematical evidence and reasoning — e.g. yes voters: "Why do you think the claim is true? What mathematical evidence supports your thinking?"; no voters: "Why do you think the claim is not true? Can you give a counterexample or other mathematical evidence?" Students question, challenge, extend, or refine one another's arguments; the teacher draws on suggested arguments and facilitation questions to introduce a missing perspective, elicit additional reasoning, or keep the discussion moving.
  - 4. Revisit the claim: Students vote again — yes, no, or undecided — and discuss what mathematical evidence or reasoning influenced their thinking.
  - 5. Name the takeaway: Students articulate what the mathematics supports and, when appropriate, refine or qualify the original claim.

Priority grouping pattern: Individual preparation → two groups or whole-class discussion. When the claim supports mathematically defensible positions, students may prepare in support and challenge/qualification groups, develop and present their cases, and then come together to evaluate the evidence and refine the claim. Use whole-class discussion instead when assigned positions are inappropriate or when the goal is to qualify the claim rather than debate opposing sides.

Illustrative examples:
  - Perimeter and area — claim: "A larger perimeter means a larger area.": Students can find examples that appear to support the claim, but counterexamples involving rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas help them refine the relationship.
      Ask: Can you find two rectangles where the one with the larger perimeter also has the larger area?
      Expected: Yes. A 3 × 4 rectangle has perimeter 14 and area 12; a 5 × 6 rectangle has perimeter 22 and area 30.
      Why: Establishes that the claim can appear reasonable based on examples.
      Ask: Can two rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas?
      Expected: Yes. A 1 × 11 rectangle and a 5 × 7 rectangle both have perimeter 24, but their areas are 11 and 35.
      Why: Surfaces a counterexample showing that perimeter and area are not directly determined by one another.
      Ask: What can we conclude about the relationship between perimeter and area from these examples?
      Expected: A larger perimeter does not necessarily mean a larger area; perimeter and area measure different attributes, and knowing one does not determine the other.
      Why: Moves beyond finding a counterexample to articulating the broader mathematical relationship.
      Takeaway: Perimeter and area measure different attributes. Knowing that one rectangle has a larger perimeter does not necessarily tell us that it has a larger area.
  - Slope — claim: "A line with a greater slope is always steeper.": Students begin with positive slopes that support the claim, then consider a negative slope that challenges it, distinguishing the magnitude of slope (steepness) from its sign (direction).
      Ask: Which is steeper: a line with slope 2 or a line with slope 5? How do you know?
      Expected: The line with slope 5 is steeper because its slope has greater magnitude.
      Why: Establishes an intuitive case that supports the claim.
      Ask: Now compare slopes 2 and −5. Which line is steeper?
      Expected: The line with slope −5 is steeper.
      Why: Provides a counterexample to the claim as stated and surfaces the distinction between slope's sign and magnitude.
      Ask: So what is misleading about the phrase 'greater slope'?
      Expected: A greater numerical slope is not necessarily a steeper slope; the absolute value of the slope determines steepness, while the sign indicates direction.
      Why: Refines the informal rule into a more precise mathematical statement.
      Takeaway: The absolute value of the slope determines steepness; the sign of the slope indicates direction.
  - Dividing fractions — claim: "Keep-Change-Flip is always the best way to divide two fractions.": Students initially support the claim because Keep-Change-Flip is reliable, then examine cases where numerators and denominators divide directly, revealing that a procedure that always works is not necessarily the most efficient strategy.
      Ask: How would you use Keep-Change-Flip to solve 21/12 ÷ 7/6? Why does this procedure work?
      Expected: Keep 21/12, change division to multiplication, and flip 7/6 to get 21/12 × 6/7.
      Why: Establishes Keep-Change-Flip as a valid and dependable procedure.
      Ask: Is there another way to look at 21/12 ÷ 7/6? What happens if we divide the two numerators and the two denominators?
      Expected: 21 ÷ 7 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, giving 3/2.
      Why: Surfaces a more direct strategy when the numerators and denominators divide evenly, and shows that the structure of the fractions can sometimes simplify the calculation.
      Ask: Does this mean Keep-Change-Flip is wrong? What should we change about the original claim?
      Expected: No. Keep-Change-Flip works, but it is not always the most efficient strategy. When the numerators and denominators divide evenly, directly simplifying the corresponding parts may be quicker.
      Why: Moves students from evaluating a procedure as simply right or wrong to considering when different strategies are useful and efficient.
      Takeaway: Keep-Change-Flip is a reliable way to divide fractions, but it is not always the most efficient strategy. When the structure of the fractions allows for direct simplification, another strategy may be quicker.

Teacher facilitation:
  Provide a small set of targeted facilitation questions tailored to the specific claim and anticipated student reasoning, with what to listen for and a follow-up move where useful. Always provide a small set of substantive arguments supporting and challenging the claim as teacher-reference material, not a script — the challenging argument may identify a counterexample, boundary condition, assumption, or limitation. Teachers prioritize students' own arguments and use suggestions selectively. Maintain a discussion in which students respond to evidence and reasoning, not to one another's opinions or confidence.
  Useful prompts:
    - Why do you think the claim is true? / Why do you think the claim is not true?
    - What mathematical evidence supports your thinking?
    - Can you give an example that supports your position?
    - Does that always work? How do you know?
    - Can anyone find a case that challenges this argument?
    - What assumptions are you making?
    - Does this argument apply to all cases or only some?
    - What would you change about the claim based on what we've found?
    - What does this example tell us about the claim?
    - Did the mathematics change your mind? Why?

Assessment context:
  - Multiple choice: Develop the claim from the misconception or distractor pattern. Identify a claim that captures the relevant mathematical idea and generate supporting and challenging arguments for the teacher to reference during discussion.
  - Open response: When authentic student responses are available, connect the claim to patterns in students' reasoning. Student responses may also provide examples, counterexamples, or arguments the teacher can bring into the discussion.

Design and implementation notes:
  - The claim should be mathematically meaningful and closely connected to the misconception, instructional need, content, and lesson context.
  - Students use mathematical evidence and reasoning to support, challenge, or refine the claim rather than simply state whether they agree.
  - The yes / no / undecided voting structure surfaces initial thinking without forcing a binary position. The initial vote should not reveal the intended resolution.
  - Generated arguments should represent meaningful mathematical reasoning rather than a "correct" argument and a deliberately weak opposing one.
  - When presenting a generated argument, the teacher invites students to evaluate, question, extend, or challenge it rather than simply accept it.
  - Arguments are mathematical objects for examination. The goal is not a "winning" side but determining what the mathematics supports and why.
  - When appropriate, the original claim should be qualified or refined rather than simply accepted or rejected.

Views:
  - Student view: Present the claim and activity without revealing the intended mathematical resolution or which arguments are strongest.
  - Teacher view: May include the suggested supporting and challenging arguments, anticipated reasoning, possible counterexamples or qualifications, facilitation guidance, and the mathematical takeaway.

Optional extension: Structured debate: when time and preparation allow, identify two teams in advance, one preparing a case supporting the claim and the other challenging or qualifying it, with generated arguments as starting points and the remaining students as an evaluating audience. Extension: students generate their own related claim, identify a counterexample or boundary condition, or revise the original claim to make it more mathematically precise.

This template is not a label applied after the fact. The activity must follow its classroom flow, its priority grouping pattern and its defining instructional move; an activity that could equally have come from another template has failed.

The move this template was selected to enact for THIS need: ask students to defend or refute the claim that satisfying one inequality is sufficient for the system, using examples and counterexamples
Why it was selected: The core misconception is conceptual — students treat a system as 'either-or' rather than requiring simultaneous satisfaction. With 9 students (32%) selecting union-like choices on Q4 (mostly Q4C) and low confidence (mean 2.33), a claim-driven task asking for evidence and counterexamples forces students to consider simultaneous truth and produce concrete counterexamples that reveal the difference between union and intersection.

## Classroom feasibility
- Require minimal setup — activity should be implementable within 30–60 seconds of classroom transition.
- Use simple, familiar instructional routines that early-career teachers can execute without extensive prep.
- Avoid complex classroom logistics: no multiple rounds of regrouping, no complicated grouping structures, no detailed classroom management procedures.
- Focus on instructional moves rather than logistics — describe what the teacher says and does, not how to move furniture.

## Pacing
The steps and the closing discussion together should take about 12 minutes of class, and never more than 15. Plan the minutes as an experienced teacher would for this class, not an ideal pace:
- Students take longer than an adult to do the math: reading the problem, working it, and checking it each take real time, so a single task worked in pairs is rarely under 3 minutes.
- Pair or small-group talk needs time to start and to wrap up; a share-out takes about a minute for each student or pair the teacher calls on.
- Every change of grouping or of materials costs time; count it in the step where it happens.
- The examples are alternatives for the teacher to choose from. Plan the time to run one with the class; the others are spares, not extra rounds.
- If the plan does not fit, cut content: fewer steps, one example, a shorter share-out. Never shrink an estimate to make the total fit.

## Math formatting
Use LaTeX for every mathematical expression: $...$ inline, $$...$$ for a standalone equation. Never use Unicode math symbols (≤ ≥ ≠ × ÷ √ π ½ ²) or caret/underscore notation outside the delimiters. Fractions are $\frac{a}{b}$, inequalities $\leq$ / $\geq$, multiplication $\times$. Write each command with ONE backslash: never \\ (a line break) or \  (a forced space), and never a placeholder symbol such as \square — write the real symbol or words instead. Plain prose stays plain English — only the math goes inside delimiters.

### Closing Discussion
The Closing Discussion should help the teacher use the activity to surface, consolidate, and extend the mathematical thinking that matters most for the identified instructional need.
Each activity includes 3 Discussion Questions, 1-3 Watch For sets, and a Mathematical Takeaway. They should be coherent with one another, grounded in the specific activity, and generated as connected components, not independently.

You are a K-12 mathematics reviewer checking the Closing Discussion of a classroom activity before teachers see it.

### Mathematical accuracy and coherence check
  - The Mathematical Takeaway is mathematically correct and supported by the activity.
  - The Discussion Questions are mathematically correct, well-posed, and aligned to the takeaway.
  - Every question's premise is mathematically valid, and its answer is correct when solved independently. A question that invites "sometimes" or "when does this work?" must have an answer whose conditions are actually true — never one that endorses an invalid move (for example, that operating on only one side of an equation can preserve equality).
  - Any anticipated answer, generalization, counterexample, or condition in the teacher guidance is mathematically accurate.
  - The Watch For sets describe plausible student thinking grounded in the activity rather than generic misconceptions.
  - The "Try asking" prompts genuinely elicit or advance mathematical reasoning rather than give away the answer.
  - The "How to respond" guidance accurately reflects the mathematics and does not assume more about student thinking than the evidence supports.
  - The three Discussion Questions and the Watch For sets collectively reinforce the same mathematical takeaway.
  - No component introduces unrelated mathematics or relies on an unstated assumption.

### Mathematical Takeaway
The mathematical understanding students should have an opportunity to develop, clarify, or recognize through the activity.
  - A concise statement of the underlying mathematical idea, relationship, principle, or reasoning — not a description of the activity steps.
  - Addresses the instructional need while remaining faithful to the actual mathematics of the activity.
  - Captures what is mathematically important beyond the particular examples or numbers used in the activity.
  - Specific enough to serve as the mathematical anchor for the Discussion Questions and Watch For sets.
  - Does not overstate a pattern or generalize beyond the conditions under which the mathematics is true.
  - Uses mathematically precise language appropriate to the students' level.
  - Does not simply say what students did: "Students compared the two strategies" describes an activity; "Different strategies can produce the same result, but they may make different assumptions or reveal different aspects of the mathematics" is a takeaway.
  - Does not simply restate the instructional need: the need describes what students need to develop or clarify; the takeaway describes the mathematical understanding that addresses it.
  - Before using it to generate the rest of the Closing Discussion, verify it is mathematically correct, appropriately precise, and supported by the activity.

### Discussion Questions (exactly 3)
Build on the mathematical thinking surfaced during the activity and help students deepen or extend the mathematical takeaway. Teachers can use, adapt, or replace them. Help students test, generalize, apply, challenge, or connect the underlying idea rather than review the activity steps, repeat worked examples, provide more practice, or introduce an unrelated skill. When possible, move beyond the original activity: whether an idea always holds, the conditions under which it does or doesn't, applying it in a new situation, or connecting it to a broader principle. Prioritize questions that reveal or develop reasoning over questions that merely elicit a correct answer.
Purposes:
  - TEST: Examine whether an idea or strategy still works when something changes.
  - GENERALIZE: Identify a pattern, relationship, condition, or rule that extends beyond the examples in the activity.
  - APPLY: Use the mathematical idea in a meaningfully different situation.
  - CHALLENGE: Find a counterexample, limitation, boundary case, or situation in which the original reasoning needs to be modified.
  - CONNECT: Connect the mathematical idea to another representation, strategy, concept, or mathematical principle.
Do not force every activity to include every type. Select the purposes that best support the mathematical takeaway.
Each question must:
  - Mathematically meaningful and connected to the mathematical takeaway.
  - Answerable using the activity, prior knowledge reasonably expected of the students, and mathematical reasoning.
  - Requires more than recall, repetition, or completion of another nearly identical example.
  - Creates an opportunity for explanation, justification, comparison, prediction, representation, construction, or transfer.
  - Appropriately open when multiple valid approaches or answers are possible.
  - Uses mathematically precise language.
  - Avoids false or unsupported generalizations.
  - Does not introduce a new mathematical skill or concept unrelated to the instructional need or takeaway.
  - Specific to the activity rather than generic.
  - No two questions elicit essentially the same reasoning.
  - If a question asks whether a claim "always" holds, the claim and its conditions must be mathematically verified. If it does not always hold, the question explicitly invites students to determine when it holds, find a counterexample, or identify the conditions.
  - Questions do not embed the intended conclusion. When students are to determine whether a claim is true, preserve that opportunity.

### Watch For, Try Asking, How to Respond
Brief, actionable teacher guidance that helps teachers anticipate student thinking, respond to what students say or do, and move the conversation forward. Selected because they are instructionally useful for the need or illuminate the takeaway — not simply because they are common misconceptions. They complement the Discussion Questions by focusing on likely in-the-moment student responses and how the teacher might respond. Not a comprehensive list: a small number of high-value student moves.
At least 1 and up to 3, prioritizing quality, relevance, and usefulness over quantity. Prefer 2-3 high-value sets when the activity supports them, but allow a single set when one response pattern is substantially more relevant than others.
Each set:
  - watchFor: One specific student move, misconception, interpretation, or productive idea the teacher may encounter. Describe what students might say, do, choose, or misunderstand, grounded in the specific thinking surfaced by the activity.
  - tryAsking: A specific, student-facing prompt to elicit, probe, clarify, challenge, or extend the student's thinking — one that helps students do the reasoning rather than leading them to the answer.
  - howToRespond: Concise guidance on how to respond to what the student says or does: affirm productive thinking, surface the reasoning, address a misconception, connect to the mathematical idea, or prompt revision. When helpful, include the anticipated idea or answer the teacher should be prepared to recognize.
Rules:
  - Each set focuses on one specific student move or misconception; do not combine unrelated misconceptions or list possible errors.
  - Asset-based: incorrect responses are understandable representations of reasoning, not evidence of deficiency. When a response contains productive thinking, help the teacher identify and build on it before addressing what needs to change.
  - Do not assume an individual student's response has a single underlying cause. Use "Students may…" or "A student might…", and give prompts that investigate the reasoning rather than asserting an inferred misconception as certain.
  - Ground each set in the specific activity, takeaway, instructional need, and student thinking represented or anticipated in the activity.
  - Focus on student thinking that is likely and instructionally consequential.
  - Prompts are open enough to elicit reasoning and do not give away the answer.
  - The teacher response is actionable, not a restatement of the misconception or the correct answer.
  - Include productive or partially correct thinking when it offers an important opportunity to build understanding.
  - Avoid generic prompts such as "Can you explain your thinking?" unless paired with a specific mathematical focus.
  - Do not duplicate the Discussion Questions: Watch For is in-the-moment thinking and teacher response; Discussion Questions are whole-class exploration of the takeaway.
  - Do not invent a misconception solely because it is common in the topic; it must connect plausibly to the reasoning students use in this activity.
  - Distinguish what is observable from what is inferred: describe what the student might say, do, choose, or represent before suggesting an interpretation.
